Work in progress

Starting a design system for DFYNE

Auditing a campaign-driven Shopify site, then building the variables and first components of a Figma design system, with accessibility built into the foundations rather than added later.

RoleUX/UI Designer. I led the audit and built the system.
CompanyDFYNE, Scottish activewear brand on Shopify Plus
ScopeLive site audit, variables (colour, type, spacing), core component library
StatusFoundations and first components built in Figma. Not yet rolled out to the live theme.
ProblemAuditFoundationsComponentsBefore and afterWhat's nextWhat I learned
01

The problem

DFYNE is a campaign-based business. New drops go live fast and traffic spikes around each one, so pages tend to get built section by section under time pressure. Over time that left the site with no shared source of truth. Values were set per section rather than pulled from shared styles.

The site looked consistent at a glance but wasn't underneath. That meant slower design and dev handover, small inconsistencies customers notice even if they can't name them, and accessibility gaps that were hard to fix one page at a time.

I wanted to give the website team one set of foundations and components to design and build from, starting with the problems that showed up most.

02

Auditing the live site

Before designing anything, I audited the live UK store to find out what the site actually uses, not what the theme intends. I checked the homepage, a collection page and a product page on desktop (1283px wide) and read every value from the browser's computed styles, so the findings reflect what customers really see.

Typography

The homepage alone used 8 font sizes and 9 letter-spacing values. The product page added three more sizes.

11.05px looks like a calculated leftover rather than a chosen step. The product page adds 15, 16.25 and 21px.

  • Font family. Raleway is the brand face, but 135 text elements on the homepage rendered in the browser's generic sans-serif, and the Klaviyo sign-up form loaded Nunito Sans.
  • Letter-spacing. 0.25, 0.3, 0.325, 1.105, 1.4, 1.5, 2.25, 2.5 and 3px all appeared. Footer H2s used 3px while other H2s used 1.5px, and "Product details" used 4.2px.
  • Missing H1. The collection page had no H1. "ALL PRODUCTS" was an H2 at 19px. The product page H1 was 21px sentence case and the homepage H1 was 30px.
  • Casing. Headings mixed CSS uppercase and sentence case at the same level. The colourway showed as "WILD BERRY" on the product page and "Wild Berry" on product cards.

Homepage section H2s were 10px while the paragraph under them was 14px. On the product page, the H3 "Recently viewed" (16.25px) was larger than the H2s above it (10px).

  • Prices were 12px black on cards and 15px #1C1D1D on the product page, so the price colour changed between the two.
  • Selectors. The UK country selector was a grey 25px box with a 4px radius, next to a pill-shaped search bar in the same header.

03

Foundations

I set the system up in two layers using Figma variables. Primitives hold raw values: every grey, every font size, every spacing step. Semantic tokens describe what a value is for and point at a primitive. Components only use the semantic layer, so a value can change in one place without hunting through every page.

PrimitiveBlack Scale/Pure Black

The raw value. Never used directly in a design.

→
Semantic tokenText/Primary

What it's for. Swaps to Pure White in dark mode.

→
ComponentButton/Secondary label

Uses the token, so it updates everywhere at once.

Colour

The semantic colour tokens are grouped into Text, Background, Stroke and Overlay. The five blacks from the audit collapse into a single Text/Primary token, with a short, deliberate grey scale for secondary, tertiary and disabled text.

Light and dark modes are set up so the structure is ready if it's ever needed, without redoing any components.

12px floor

Caption and Label are the smallest steps at 12px, replacing the 9px text used on live buttons and badges.

Mobile and desktop

Headings scale between breakpoints through modes, so there's one token per role instead of separate mobile styles.

+25% modes

Every step scales up by roughly a quarter, so I can design and test for people who enlarge text, in line with WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text).

Spacing

Spacing tokens are grouped by how they're used rather than by size, so it's clear which one to pick:

  • Inset: padding inside components
  • Stack: vertical gaps between elements
  • Inline: horizontal gaps
  • Heading: space above and below each heading size
  • Layout: page margins, gutters and sections
  • Target size (accessibility): 24px minimum, in line with WCAG 2.2 AA (2.5.8), and 44px touch, in line with AAA (2.5.5)

Most steps follow a 4 and 8px rhythm and change between mobile and desktop.

04

Components

With the foundations in place, I started on the components the audit showed were the most inconsistent or most used.

Button

The top priority, since the live site had nine variations doing the same job.

  • One component, 23 variants: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary and Link across Default, Hover, Pressed, Focus and Disabled, plus an icon-only Quick Add button with three states.
  • One default height of 40px, hugging its content, with 12/24px padding.
  • Everything bound to variables: spacing, colour and typography.
  • Flexible without detaching: editable label, and either icon can be toggled or swapped.
  • Readable labels: 12px Label token instead of the live site's 9px.

Testing components together

To check the selection components work in a real layout rather than just on a component sheet, I built a filter panel from them and laid out each state: closed, sort options, product type, fit, colour, size and leg length.

06

What's next

This is the start of the system, not the finished thing. These are the gaps I know about and what I'd do next:

  • Radius tokens. Reduce the live site's radius values to a short scale: 0, 4px and full.
  • Letter-spacing tokens. The audit found nine tracking values. These aren't tokenised yet.
  • Feedback colours. Add semantic tokens for the alert colours rather than relying on primitives, and review the naming of the critical and error variants.
  • Colour filter swatches. Map them to real DFYNE colourways instead of generic colours.
  • Badge component. One shape and type style with variants for New, Limited Edition and Sale.
  • Focus states. One consistent, clearly visible focus style across every button type.
  • Touch targets. Decide whether the 40px default button should move to the 44px touch token.
  • Rollout. Work with the developers to bring tokens into the Shopify theme, starting with buttons and type, and fix the heading structure as part of the wider accessibility work.
07

What I learned

  • Audit first. Reading computed styles from the live site gave me evidence rather than opinions, and made it much easier to explain why the system was needed.
  • Semantic naming matters more than the values. Getting the structure right early means values can change later without breaking components.
  • Accessibility belongs in the foundations. Building the 12px floor, text scaling modes and target sizes into the variables means every component inherits them, rather than fixing each page afterwards.
  • Start small. Prioritising the five biggest problems kept the scope realistic alongside day-to-day campaign work.
Mathew Sinclair · UX/UI Designer · DFYNE Design System case study, work in progress, November 2026
